Guenther's vole (Microtus guentheri) exhibits a reproductive strategy characterized by relatively modest litter sizes and a rapid developmental schedule under typical physiological conditions. Field observations indicate that females typically produce litters containing 6 pups [N_R_i = litters containing 6 pups] during a breeding event. When considering the annual cycle, the maximum reproductive rate translates to roughly 3.3 litters per year [F_R_i = roughly 3.3 litters per year], a frequency that reflects the species' ability to exploit seasonal resource pulses in its Mediterranean grassland and agricultural habitats. These values were recorded from individuals maintained at a core body temperature of 38.3 °C [T = 38.3 °C], which is the standard thermal condition for active, non-stressed animals of this species. The combination of 6 pups per litter and 3.3 litters per year results in a daily reproduction rate of approximately 0.054 pups per day [Ri = approximately 0.054 pups per day], though this figure is expressed per annum for biological clarity. Compared to other Microtus species of similar size, this reproductive output is moderate and likely constrained by the energetic demands of sustaining high metabolic rates in a variable climate. The interplay between litter size and breeding frequency underscores the vole's capacity for rapid population growth under favorable conditions, a trait common among arvicoline rodents inhabiting unpredictable environments.

Neonatal development in Guenther's vole begins with a brief intrauterine phase, as gestation proceeds for only 21 days [tg = 21 days] when the mother maintains a temperature of 38.3 °C [T = 38.3 °C]. This short gestation is typical for small-bodied microtines and is offset by the altricial state of the newborns at parturition. Newborn pups weigh a mere 3 grams [Wwb = 3 grams] at birth, a modest initial mass that necessitates intensive maternal investment during the early postnatal period. Lactation proceeds rapidly, and the pups gain weight quickly on a diet of highly nutritious milk. The mother's metabolic rate increases substantially during this phase to support milk synthesis. The brief gestation, coupled with the low birth mass, allows females to allocate resources efficiently across multiple reproductive bouts within a single breeding season, contributing to the species' high annual output when environmental conditions are permissive.

The suckling stage is a critical period of growth and development for Microtus guentheri juveniles. Under the thermal conditions typical of active metabolic periods in this species (38.3 °C [T = 38.3 °C]), pups are weaned at 18 days after birth [tx = 18 days after birth], marking the transition from complete dependence on maternal milk to the consumption of solid plant material. By the time of nutritional independence, the young voles have achieved a wet weight at weaning of 15 grams [Wwx = 15 grams], representing a fivefold increase from their neonatal mass. This rapid pre-weaning growth trajectory is energetically demanding for the lactating female, who must consume large quantities of green vegetation and grains to meet her own maintenance requirements and those of the litter. The body mass attained at weaning is a critical determinant of subsequent survival and growth rates, as heavier juveniles typically enjoy a competitive advantage when foraging independently in the field.

Sexual maturation in Guenther's vole exhibits a pronounced sexual dimorphism in timing, a pattern documented in several Microtus species. Females reach puberty at 60 days after birth [tp = 60 days after birth] when maintained at a body temperature of 38.3 °C [T = 38.3 °C], whereas males require a longer developmental period and attain sexual maturity at 95 days after birth [tp = 95 days after birth] under identical thermal conditions. This difference in maturation time likely reflects the contrasting selective pressures acting on the two sexes: females benefit from early reproduction to maximize lifetime fecundity in a short-lived species, while males may require additional time to achieve the body size necessary for successful competition for access to estrous females. The onset of puberty in both sexes coincides with the attainment of a substantial proportion of the ultimate adult body mass, which reaches an ultimate wet weight of 51.9 grams [Wwi = 51.9 grams].

Lifespan and body size parameters place Microtus guentheri within the typical range for small arvicoline rodents inhabiting seasonal Mediterranean environments. The maximum recorded longevity for this species is approximately 3.9 years [am = approximately 3.9 years] under field conditions where the animals maintain a body temperature of 38.3 °C [T = 38.3 °C]. This life span is consistent with that of other vole species of comparable ultimate wet weight, which reaches 51.9 grams [Wwi = 51.9 grams] in adults. The relatively short life expectancy, combined with the early age at first reproduction, results in a life history strategy that emphasizes high reproductive output over extended survival. Mortality rates are highest during the first few weeks after weaning, when juveniles are most vulnerable to predation and environmental stress. Adult survival is also influenced by the availability of high-quality forage and the intensity of territorial interactions among breeding males, factors that can dramatically alter population dynamics from year to year.
